name: Polycarp of Smyrna

born.date: c. 69 (based on his words at his trial that he had served Christ for 86 years)
born.place: Probably Smyrna, Asia Minor (modern İzmir, Turkey)

died.place: The stadium of Smyrna, Asia Minor (modern İzmir, Turkey)
died.cause: Martyred: condemned to be burned, then stabbed

summary: Bishop of Smyrna, said by Irenaeus to have been taught by the apostle John, whose execution in old age is recorded in the Martyrdom of Polycarp, the earliest surviving account of a Christian martyrdom after the New Testament. He is one of the "Apostolic Fathers," the earliest Christian writers after the New Testament (c. 90–150).

key_dates.label: Receives Ignatius on his way to Rome; writes his Letter to the Philippians
Visits Rome to discuss the date of Easter with Bishop Anicetus

accomplishments.text: Is described by his pupil Irenaeus as a disciple of the apostle John and of others who had seen Jesus, making him a living link between the apostles and the later 2nd-century church.
Wrote a Letter to the Philippians, full of quotations from New Testament writings, which also preserves Ignatius's letters for the church at Philippi.
Led the church in Smyrna for decades and received a letter from Ignatius of Antioch addressed to him personally.

Traveled to Rome in old age to discuss with Bishop Anicetus the different dates on which churches celebrated Easter. They did not agree, but stayed in communion, and Anicetus let him celebrate the Eucharist in Rome.
Opposed the teacher Marcion, reportedly calling him "the firstborn of Satan."
His martyrdom account is the first to describe Christians keeping the anniversary of a martyr's death and honoring his remains, the beginning of the cult of the saints.

original.phrase: "Eighty-six years I have served him, and he has done me no wrong. How then can I blaspheme my King who saved me?"
original.reference: Martyrdom of Polycarp 9, his reply to the proconsul
original.note: Recorded by the church of Smyrna shortly after his death.

persecution_note: Polycarp was arrested during an outbreak of persecution in Smyrna, in which other Christians had already been killed by wild beasts. He refused to swear by the emperor's "genius" and curse Christ, and was burned and then stabbed in the stadium. The Martyrdom of Polycarp, written by the church of Smyrna, blames the crowd of both pagans and Jews. Scholars note that this account reflects the tensions of its time, and they debate how far its picture of Jewish involvement is accurate.

persecution.title: Arrest, trial, and execution in Smyrna
persecution.summary: After the crowd in the stadium demanded that Polycarp be found, the police captain Herod sent men who found him at a farm outside the city. Brought before the proconsul, he refused to swear by the emperor's genius or to revile Christ. The crowd asked the Asiarch Philip to set a lion on him, but he refused because the animal games were over. The crowd then demanded that he be burned. According to the account, the flames formed an arch around him without harming him, so an executioner stabbed him, and his body was then burned.

responsible.name: Lucius Statius Quadratus
responsible.role: Proconsul (Roman governor) of Asia; tried and condemned him

responsible.name: Herod
responsible.role: Police captain (eirenarch) of Smyrna; arrested him

responsible.name: Nicetes
responsible.role: Herod's father; urged him to submit

responsible.name: Philip the Asiarch
responsible.role: Official in charge of the games; declined to set a lion on him

responsible.name: Crowd in the stadium
responsible.role: Pagans and, according to the account, Jews of Smyrna who demanded his death

responsible.name: Executioner
responsible.role: Stabbed him when the fire did not kill him

persecution.outcome: Killed at about 86 years old. The church of Smyrna gathered his bones and kept the anniversary of his death.

excommunication_note: No excommunication or condemnation of him is recorded. His disagreement with Bishop Anicetus of Rome over the date of Easter did not lead to any break in communion.
